title: Twenty-Two Years Later, the 'Mohra' Couple Is Back. The Whole 'Welcome To The Jungle' Set Stood Up and Clapped.
excerpt: Akshay Kumar and Raveena Tandon reunite on screen for the first time since 2004 in Ahmed Khan's stacked Friday comedy — not as lovers this time, but with a song and a lot of history.
body:
It started with a girlfriend and a hand pump in 1994, and somehow it ends — three decades later — with the whole crew of Welcome To The Jungle breaking into applause on set. When Akshay Kumar and Raveena Tandon finally danced together again in front of the cameras, Suniel Shetty wandered onto the floor, took one look, and said it for everybody: "Arre, mere Mohra ki jodi aa gayi." My Mohra couple is back.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=R704yP3dlXw

That's the emotional center of the third Welcome, which storms into cinemas worldwide this Friday, June 26. On paper it's a comedy juggernaut — director Ahmed Khan has crammed in what feels like half of Bollywood: Akshay, Suniel, Paresh Rawal, Arshad Warsi, Jackie Shroff, Rajpal Yadav, Jacqueline Fernandez, Disha Patani, and a roll call of familiar faces deep enough to fill a wedding hall. But the talking point that's outrun every gag in the trailer is the one piece of casting nobody saw as just casting: the reunion of a couple Bollywood spent the entire 1990s gossiping about.

Akshay and Raveena were the pairing of that decade — Mohra, the chemistry, the speculation, the reported engagement, the eventual split that launched a thousand tabloid covers. Their last film together was Police Force: An Inside Story in 2004. Twenty-two years of silence, separate lives, separate families. And then Ahmed Khan, who's known both of them for thirty years, decided to just... put them back in the same frame.

"People will want to see Raveena and Akshay together, so why not do a fan service?" — Ahmed Khan, director

He makes it sound easy, but he's also the only person who could have pulled it off, precisely because he knows where every body is buried. "Both Raveena and Akshay have been such good friends of mine," he told Mid-Day. "Because we go back so long, we know what has happened in each other's lives." When he floated the idea to Raveena, expecting hesitation, he got none. Her reply has the kind of grown-up swagger that makes you root for her: "So what? We are all actors and grown up. We are all friends and we will have a blast on the sets." Reader, that is how you close a chapter.

They don't play romantic leads this time — the years have rerouted that particular current — but Khan wasn't about to waste the nostalgia. He's given them a full song sequence, choreographed by Rahul Shetty and Prince Gupta, and by every account on set it was the moment the production held its breath. Two stars who once lit up the same screen, older now, talking between takes about their kids ("Everyone progresses," Khan recalled), then snapping into a dance number like no time had passed. If the film does nothing else, that sequence is going to wreck the millennials who grew up on Mohra.

Around that beating heart, Welcome To The Jungle is selling pure, unembarrassed masala. The trailer is loud, garish, and proudly nonsensical — exactly the register Akshay rules. This is his most reliable lane: the commercial comedy entertainer, the genre that built him into one of the most bankable names in the industry. After the modest run of his last outing, he needs the Welcome franchise's nostalgic pull to do its job. The franchise itself has been dormant since 2007's original and its 2015 sequel, so there's nearly two decades of brand goodwill being cashed in at once.

The trade is cautious. Advance bookings point to a respectable rather than thunderous start — projections hover in the ₹15–20 crore net range for opening day, with paid previews potentially nudging things up if word of mouth catches. Comedy ensembles live or die on the weekend family crowd, and a film this stacked with veterans is built precisely for the multi-generational outing. There's also a side debate simmering online about how much the premise borrows from Hollywood's Tropic Thunder — a comparison the makers will happily ignore all the way to the box office if the laughs land.

For the diaspora, Welcome To The Jungle releases in cinemas across the US, UK, Canada, and the Gulf the same day as India, the standard wide overseas rollout Akshay's films command — so the Friday-night NRI multiplex run is on. A streaming home will follow in the usual weeks-later window, almost certainly on the platform that's become Bollywood's default OTT destination.

But forget the numbers for a second. The real ticket here is sentimental: a generation that swooned over Mohra gets to watch its couple share a frame one more time, not as lovers, but as two people who made peace and came back to play. Sometimes the best fan service isn't a cameo or a callback. Sometimes it's just two old co-stars, dancing, while the whole set claps.
